idiom_name: final class conforming to the collaborator protocol with configurable state
implementation_notes: XCTest ships no mocking facility and Swift has no reflection-based double generation at runtime, so the reusable double is written by hand: a final class conforms to the collaborator protocol, stores the answers the test configures (plain properties or closures) and optionally records the calls it received for later assertions. Protocols are the substitution seam because Swift prefers protocol-typed dependencies and structs cannot be subclassed, so the double is simply another conforming type. Use it for small protocols and existing code; reach for a generator only when the protocol is wide.
pitfalls: Members of struct-typed dependencies cannot be replaced at all; if the collaborator is a struct or a final class used concretely, refactoring the dependency to a protocol is the prerequisite for any double.
A fake holding closures that capture the test case strongly keeps the test object alive and can turn a leak-free suite into one with retained fixtures.
Because the fake is hand-written, a protocol change surfaces as a compile error in the fake, which is desirable - but a fake copied between targets can drift from the protocol of another module.

variants.name: Mockingbird generated mocks with given(...).willReturn(...)
variants.implementation_notes: Because Swift lacks the runtime reflection needed to fabricate a double, toolkits such as Mockingbird and Cuckoo generate a mock type from the protocol at build time (mockingbird configure/generate, or a Cuckoo build phase) and the test configures it with given(clock.now()).willReturn(epoch), verifying with verify(clock.now()).wasCalled(). The generated mock is the reusable double and the given/verify DSL is the configuration interface; the trade-off is a build step and a generated file that must be regenerated whenever the protocol changes, which is the statically generated route of the pattern.
pitfalls: The generated mock is checked in and silently drifts from the protocol unless the generator runs as part of the test target's build.
Generators only mock protocols (and, with restrictions, classes), so sealed framework types still need a protocol seam around them.
Generated mocks add build time and a dependency that must be kept compatible with the Swift toolchain version.
